And he himself also said somewhere in evangelical writings: ‘If in the moist wood they did these things, in the dry what will they do?’ naming himself a moist and well-flowering wood. And a wood is shown to divine Moses from beside God. For the Father alone reveals the Son, since he alone also knows him. ‘For no one knows who the Son is, except the Father.’ Therefore in Christos / Christ the wood of life, the bitter things are sweet, the hard-to-bear are bearable, and the things that in their own nature are accustomed to corrupt become necessary unto life. Palladius: In what manner do you say? Cyril: If indeed it is true that the toils, being very bitter, corrupt the body, yet make the soul a sharer of the eternal life (and Paul also said somewhere: ‘When I am weak, then I am powerful.’ And again: ‘For if our outer human is being corrupted, yet the inner is being renewed day by day’)—who would ever choose to endure through toils so sharp, unless having the sweet hope that is in Christos / Christ? Palladius: No one would, I think, altogether. Cyril: See therefore already (for it is necessary for us, Palladius, to go toward remembrance of the things at the beginnings) Israel having thirsted in a desert, and murmuring against all-wise Moses, yet having fallen into this smallness of soul without penalty; for he did not pay justice, nor undergo the things from anger, although God is accustomed to chastise those condemned upon this. For in the beginnings the one still in the trainings for virtue is sometimes even pitied when stumbling; yet after this he has the too-great smallness of soul unpardoned, and the unbridled running-away which he might make perhaps into out-of-place desires.
